title: What Really Happened At Bastogne: 'Nuts!' And The Siege Of The 101st
sources: US Army Center of Military History: Cole, The Ardennes: Battle of the Bulge (US Army in WWII); army.mil 101st Airborne / Bastogne histories
Ultimatum text and 'NUTS!' reply (22 Dec 1944) and McAuliffe's Christmas message (24 Dec 1944) as published by the US Army
army.mil: 'Cobra King led 4th Armored Division column that relieved Bastogne' (Lt Charles Boggess, C Co 37th Tank Bn, met A Co 326th Airborne Engineers, 26 Dec 1944)
Time magazine 1945: Distinguished Unit Citation never before awarded to an entire Army division
Footage: US Army Signal Corps / NARA (public domain); US Army photos (public domain)
Hedged in script: 'something like' Aw nuts (staff recollection); Harper 'go to hell' (his account); Manteuffel 'reportedly' furious; ~100 miles; ~19,000 dead; no exact clock time for the link-up

beats.text: In December 1944, a small Belgian town called Bastogne was surrounded by the German army.
Inside were American paratroopers with little ammunition, no winter coats, and no way out.
Then the Germans sent a letter asking them to surrender. The American general answered with one word.
The films make it look like a perfect Hollywood line. The real story is messier, colder, and a lot more surprising.
By late 1944, most people thought the war in the West was almost over. Paris was free. German forces had been pushed back to their own border.
The Ardennes forest in Belgium was treated as a quiet place. Tired units were sent there to rest. New units were sent there to learn.
Hitler chose exactly that place for his last great gamble.
On the sixteenth of December, in fog and snow, more than two hundred thousand German soldiers attacked.
The plan was to split the Allies in two and race all the way to the port of Antwerp.
The bad weather was part of the plan. Allied planes could not fly in it.
As the German attack pushed forward, the American line bent backward into a huge bulge on the map. That is how the battle got its name.

v.q: Battle of the Bulge map December 1944

beats.text: And in the middle of that bulge sat Bastogne.
It was not a big town. But seven main roads met there. Whoever held Bastogne controlled the roads through the Ardennes.
There was no fresh army nearby to hold it. So the Allies sent the only reserve they had.
The 101st Airborne Division was resting in France after months of fighting in Holland. Many of its men were on leave in Paris.
They were loaded onto open trucks and driven north through the night, about a hundred miles, many without proper winter clothing.
Even their commander was missing. General Maxwell Taylor was in the United States.
So the division was led by its artillery chief, Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe.
They were not alone. Tank crews of the 10th Armored Division had already raced in, and the tank destroyers of the 705th followed.
Small teams of tanks were pushed out to villages around the town to slow the enemy down. At Noville, one team held for almost two days.
Those hours gave the paratroopers time to dig in.
By the twenty first of December, every road out of Bastogne was cut.
The paratroopers liked to joke that they were used to being surrounded. Dropping behind enemy lines was their job.
But being used to it did not make it easier.
The cold was brutal. Men slept in frozen holes in the ground. Some lined their boots with newspaper.
Ammunition ran so low that some guns were limited to a handful of shells a day.
Medical supplies ran low too. The division's field hospital had been captured early in the battle.
Then, on the twenty second of December, four German soldiers walked up the road under a white flag.
They were met by men of the 327th Glider Infantry, and the two officers were taken, blindfolded, to a command post.
They carried a typed letter from a German general.
It said the fortune of war was changing. It offered the Americans one way to avoid total destruction.

v.text: the honorable surrender of the encircled town

beats.text: They had two hours to decide. If they refused, German artillery would wipe them out.
The letter was carried to McAuliffe, who had been asleep.
According to the officers in the room, he read it and said something like, us surrender? Aw, nuts.

v.by: McAuliffe, as recalled by his staff

beats.text: Then he had to send a formal reply, and he did not know what to write.
One of his officers, Lieutenant Colonel Harry Kinnard, pointed out that what he had just said would be hard to beat.
So the reply was typed on a sheet of paper. To the German commander. Nuts. The American commander.
Colonel Joseph Harper took it back to the Germans waiting on the road.
The German officers did not understand it. Was this a yes or a no?
Harper explained. In plain English, he said, it means go to hell.

v.text: In plain English, it is the same as go to hell.

beats.text: Here is the twist the films leave out. The German army commander, Hasso von Manteuffel, was reportedly furious that the letter had been sent at all.
He did not have the artillery to carry out the threat. The Germans had promised something they could not deliver.
The great bombardment never came the way the letter promised. Instead came bombers.
But first, the sky changed.
For days, fog had kept almost every Allied plane on the ground. On the twenty third of December, the skies cleared.
General George Patton had even had a prayer for good weather printed for his troops. Whether you call it luck or prayer, the weather finally broke.
Pathfinders jumped in first to guide the planes. Then the cargo planes came, wave after wave.
Parachutes filled the sky over Bastogne. Ammunition, food, medicine.
Fighter bombers attacked German tanks around the town. For the first time in days, the defenders could hit back from the air.
On Christmas Eve, McAuliffe sent his men a message. It printed the German letter and his reply.
It said, we have stopped cold everything that has been thrown at us.

v.text: We have stopped cold everything that has been thrown at us.

beats.text: That same night, German bombers hit the town. One bomb struck an aid station full of wounded men.
A Belgian nurse, Renée Lemaire, was killed. Another, Augusta Chiwy, kept treating the wounded through the siege.
On Christmas morning, German tanks and infantry attacked from the west. Some broke through the outer line.
Paratroopers and tank destroyers stopped them. The line held.
Meanwhile, the rescue was already on its way. And that part of the story starts days earlier, in a cold room in Verdun.
On the nineteenth of December, General Eisenhower met his commanders. He asked how soon anyone could attack north.
Patton said he could attack in about two days, with three divisions. Some in the room thought he was joking.
He was not. His staff had already drawn up plans in case it happened.
Tens of thousands of men and vehicles turned ninety degrees and drove north through snow and ice.
At the front of it was the 4th Armored Division. In its lead tank battalion was Lieutenant Colonel Creighton Abrams.
On the twenty sixth of December, they fought through the village of Assenois, just south of Bastogne.
The lead tank was a Sherman called Cobra King, commanded by Lieutenant Charles Boggess.
Late that afternoon, Cobra King reached a line of American foxholes. They belonged to the engineers of the 101st.
The siege was broken. Supplies and ambulances began moving into the town.
Now here is the part that started an argument that lasted for decades. Did the 101st need to be rescued?
Many of the paratroopers always said no. They said they were holding fine on their own.
The tank crews said they had fought hard to reach them. Both were true.
And the fighting was not over. Some of the hardest battles around Bastogne came in January, in the woods outside the town.
By the end, the Battle of the Bulge had cost the United States about nineteen thousand dead. It was the largest battle the US Army fought in the war.
Hitler's gamble failed. It used up tanks and men that Germany could never replace.
The 101st Airborne received the Distinguished Unit Citation. It was the first time the award went to an entire division.
McAuliffe's one word reply became one of the most famous lines of the war.
Today, Bastogne has a square named after him, with an American tank parked in it. And every December, the town holds a Nuts weekend.
So how true is the famous version? The courage is true. The cold is true. The reply really was one word.
But the full story is bigger. A quiet sector, a hundred miles in open trucks, an empty threat, a clear sky, and a tank called Cobra King.
